title: Nasdaq-100 Futures Slip as Alphabet Shares Plunge Post‑Earnings Report – Live CNBC Updates
body:
U.S. equity futures slipped early Thursday as investors processed a soft earnings report from Alphabet, the parent company of Google, which sent the tech giant’s shares tumbling and pulled down the broader Nasdaq‑100 index. Nasdaq‑100 futures were down about 1.4%, while the S&P 500 futures slipped 0.5%; the Dow futures, less exposed to the tech sector, inched up 0.3%. The market reaction underscores lingering concerns about the pace of growth in the “hyperscaler” segment of the technology industry, where the biggest cloud and AI players have been expected to sustain double‑digit expansion.

Alphabet posted third‑quarter results that fell short of analysts’ expectations on several key metrics. Revenue grew 6% year‑over‑year to $74.6 billion, lagging behind the consensus estimate of roughly $75.5 billion. More striking was the earnings per share figure, which came in at $1.23 versus the projected $1.38. The company also warned that advertising demand—a core driver of its historic profitability—remains “soft” in several regions, even as it continues to invest heavily in artificial‑intelligence initiatives and its cloud platform, Google Cloud. While the cloud segment posted a 21% revenue increase, it still lagged behind rivals such as Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, leaving investors uneasy about Alphabet’s ability to capture a larger slice of the lucrative enterprise market.

The earnings miss reverberated beyond Alphabet, rattling other hyperscalers that reported around the same time. Microsoft and Amazon, both of which posted stronger‑than‑expected cloud growth, saw their shares rise modestly, but the overall sentiment in the sector remained cautious. Traders are now weighing whether the broader slowdown in advertising spend—driven by tighter corporate budgets and a shift toward performance‑based marketing—will translate into a more sustained drag on revenue for the sector’s largest players. Moreover, the heightened competition for AI talent and the escalating cost of data‑center infrastructure have added pressure on profit margins, prompting investors to scrutinize the balance sheets of these capital‑intensive firms more closely.

Analysts highlighted that Alphabet’s “Other Bets” segment, which includes its Waymo autonomous‑driving unit and various moonshot projects, continues to operate at a loss, further weighing on the company’s bottom line. The firm’s CFO, Ruth Porat, emphasized that the company remains committed to long‑term investments in AI and cloud, but she also signaled a more disciplined approach to capital allocation in the coming quarters. This dual message—aggressive growth in emerging technologies paired with tighter cost control—has left the market uncertain about the timing and magnitude of future earnings upside.

Investors are also watching macro‑economic variables that could amplify the earnings pressure. The Federal Reserve’s ongoing rate‑hiking cycle has begun to tighten discretionary spending, a trend that could dampen ad budgets across the board. At the same time, the lingering effects of supply‑chain disruptions continue to inflate the cost of building and maintaining the massive data‑center infrastructure that underpins cloud services. If these headwinds persist, they could further compress margins for hyperscalers, making the sector’s growth trajectory more volatile than previously anticipated.

Looking ahead, the market will be closely monitoring Alphabet’s next earnings release, expected in early February, for signs that its AI‑driven products—such as the Bard chatbot and new generative‑AI tools for Workspace—are beginning to generate meaningful revenue streams. Analysts will also be keen to see whether Google Cloud can close the gap with its larger rivals, potentially through strategic partnerships or pricing adjustments. In the meantime, the dip in futures suggests that traders remain wary, but the relatively modest decline in the broader market indicates that the fallout may be contained to the tech‑heavy Nasdaq. As the earnings season progresses, the ability of the hyperscalers to translate heavy R&D spending into profitable growth will be a decisive factor for market sentiment and for the direction of U.S. equity futures in the weeks to come.
